doc.title: Indexes
doc.paragraph: An index lets an adapter answer a query from a sorted list of keys instead of reading every object of a type. Indexes are optional: an adapter returns the same objects for a query with or without them, only faster with them. This chapter describes how to define indexes, what they mean in a query, and how to see whether a query used one.
Indexes are provided by the LMDB adapter. Index functions on an adapter that does not support indexes fail with unable to get index interface.

section.title: Index Definitions
section.paragraph: An index definition has a key, the name queries use, and optionally:

list.item: objectType: the object types it applies to. Without it, it applies to every object type.
value: a script that computes the values to index. Without it, the property named by the key is indexed.
filter: a script that decides whether an object is indexed.
options: how values are compared and stored (see Options below).

section.paragraph: Definitions are not part of the adapter's configuration entry. The adapter stores them in its own database, so they last across restarts and move with the database files. They are managed with three functions:

column.literal: index_create(adapterId, key, value, objectType, filter, options, test)

row.column: Adds a definition and indexes the objects already in the database, so a query the index answers finds them too; objects written later are indexed as they are written. With test true it only checks the definition and counts what it would index: nothing is saved.
Returns the definitions, as an object keyed by index key, optionally only those for one object type.
Removes a definition and its keys.

section.paragraph: The full parameter descriptions are in the function reference, category indexes.

Definitions are read from the database in each transaction, so every process using it sees a change from its next request: a server answers its next query with the new index, and its writes keep the index up to date. A process that did not create the index's database answers queries on it by reading every object of the type, with the same results, until it next writes such an object or restarts. Index functions can be run:

list.item: In the Administrative Web App, open Admin, Services, select the LMDB adapter's service, and use its Indexes tab to list, add and remove indexes.
From a script run by afwfcgi, such as the Fiddle tool or a POST /afw action.
With the afw command, for example:

section.paragraph: A create returns how many objects it read and indexed, for example { "num_processed": 3, "num_indexed": 3 }. Creating a key that already exists returns { "message": "An index definition by this key already exists." } and changes nothing; remove it first to redefine it.

Two kinds of index made before this release can quietly miss objects, so a query that uses one returns fewer objects than the same query without the index. Earlier releases let index_create skip the objects already in the database, and the Administrative Web App's Add Index dialog did that by default, so its indexes held only objects written after they were created. Earlier releases also never put an empty string into an index, so eq "" found nothing through it. If you have indexes from an earlier release, remove each one with index_remove and create it again; the new create indexes every existing object, empty strings included. A script that still calls index_create with eight arguments now fails with too many parameters: the old retroactive argument is gone.

section.title: Options

row.column: Strings are compared without regard to case, in every relation on the key, match included. With it on sn, sn eq "HOPPER" finds "Hopper".
Each value may be held by one object only. A write that would give a second object the same value fails.
The index keeps its keys in reverse order.

The index holds numbers. A query value given as a string, as every value in a query string is, is compared as that number. Without the option, that happens only when an object type declares the property's data type; the option must agree with such a declaration. When a query value does not convert to a number, each object the index finds is tested against the query instead.

section.paragraph: unique and sort-reverse fix how the index's database is created. After index_remove, creating the same key again with different values of these options needs a restart of the application first; index_create says so when it happens.

section.title: Computed Indexes
section.paragraph: An index with a value script defines a computed name: a name objects do not have, whose value for each object is what the script returns. Queries on that name mean what the script gives, whether the adapter answers them from the index or by reading objects. While the scripts run, these variables describe the object being indexed:
A script that only reads a property can be written as is, such as current::object.givenName. A script with an operator or an array literal needs return:
A filter script returns a boolean and limits the objects that have a value under the name. Objects the filter leaves out have no value, so no relation on the name is true for them:
index_create enforces these rules:

list.item: A filter needs a value script. A filter on a plain property index would hide objects that have the property from queries.
A computed name must not be a property declared by an object type in objectType. If an object type declares it later, queries on it fail until the conflict is removed.

For an object type that declares its properties, a query may only name declared properties unless the object type's otherProperties allows queries, so a computed name on such an object type needs that.

section.paragraph: Scripts run on every write of an object the index applies to. A script that throws makes the write fail, so guard properties that may be missing, as ?? 0 does above.

section.title: How Queries Use Indexes
section.paragraph: The adapter uses an index when it can answer the filter from indexed keys, and reads every object of the type otherwise. In both cases the same objects are returned.

list.item: A relation on an indexed key can use the index when it is eq, lt, le, gt, ge, or a match that asks for values starting with some text. The pattern must be anchored and plain: ^appl or ^appl.* can use the index, but appl (which matches the text anywhere in the value) or ^ap+l cannot, and those read every object of the type.
An and can use the index when one of its terms can; the objects found are then tested against the other terms.
An or can use indexes only when every term can. An object found by more than one term is returned once.
The empty string is a value like any other and can be found with eq "".

section.paragraph: Indexes on properties whose values are arrays hold one key per element. At present a query on such a property can return different objects depending on whether the adapter used the index, so do not rely on queries of array-valued properties yet.
section.header: Seeing which plan a query used
section.paragraph: Set the trace flag trace:adapterId: followed by the adapter id to log how each retrieve was answered:
section.code: flag_set(["trace:adapterId:lmdb"], true); retrieve_objects("lmdb", "Person", { filter: { op: "eq", property: "sn", value: "HOPPER" } });
retrieve_objects: using index query index query test: sn through its index definition (case-insensitive)
section.paragraph: A query that could not use an index logs retrieve_objects: using full scan (not sargable). Add an index on a key that such queries use often.

section.title: Tuning
section.paragraph: When a query combines several indexed terms, the LMDB adapter estimates how many keys each term matches and orders the terms by that estimate, which reduces the work of removing duplicate results. The adapter configuration's index property chooses how range and "starts with" terms are estimated. It changes only the order in which indexes are read, never which objects are returned, and the default suits most databases.
section.code: { type : "adapter", adapterId : "lmdb", adapterType : "lmdb", index : { cardinalityStrategy : "probe", cardinalityProbeCap : 100 }, ... }
